title: Why Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg on Hven
topic: Why Tycho Brahe built a brass observatory on the island of Hven (Denmark, 1576) to avoid magnetic interference

lines: Tycho Brahe measured stars by eye, then built a castle around them.
Tycho's naked-eye readings had to be exact.
King Frederick II wanted to keep this famous astronomer in Denmark.
Tycho's father wanted him to practice law.
Tycho chose astronomy and complained that society wasted his time.
Frederick II heard about Tycho's plans to leave Denmark.
So the king offered Hven and funding in 1576.
Tycho began building Uraniborg in 1576 and moved there soon after.
As lord of Hven, he made farmers grow twice as much and build his castle.
The farmers complained about heavy taxes and took Tycho to court.
The court backed Tycho's right to tax and demand labor.
You see, it is like needing silence to finish one hard puzzle.
Tycho chose Hven for seclusion and royal support.
Quiet helped Tycho focus on his observations.
Tycho used quadrants, sextants, and clocks to watch the sky.
A brass plumb line helped him adjust his instruments for accuracy.
Tycho wanted to find the errors hidden inside his own instruments.
Years later, Tycho dug a second observatory underground.
Even his island instruments were not enough.
Kepler later used Tycho's careful observations to write three laws about how planets move.

claims.claim: King Frederick II offered Tycho the island of Hven and funding to set up an observatory in 1576, because he wanted to keep the distinguished scientist in Denmark.
Uraniborg's location on Hven was chosen for seclusion and support, giving Tycho a better way to focus on accurate observation without interruptions.

As lord of Hven, Tycho required the peasants to cultivate twice as much and exacted labor for the construction of his castle; the peasants complained about his taxation and took him to court, and the court established his right to levy taxes and labor.
Tycho's instruments were adjusted via a brass plumb line and thumb screws, which helped him make more accurate measurements of the heavens.
Tycho emphasized the need to determine instrumental errors.
Tycho later worked underground at Stjerneborg, where he realized his instruments in Uraniborg were not sufficient.
Johannes Kepler used Tycho's data to develop his three laws of planetary motion.
